newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's army chief denies dirty tricks claims.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's army chief denies dirty tricks claims.

text.p: South African army chief General Georg Meiring on Friday rejected accusations before the country's truth commission implicating him in violent crimes against the black opposition under apartheid.

Meiring, who was appointed by President Nelson Mandela to lead the military's transformation into a fully non-racial force, said he would hold talks with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) to discuss the issue.

The TRC, probing apartheid atrocities, told reporters on Thursday that Meiring's name was on a list of over 60 soldiers implicated in dirty tricks, including state-sponsored murder, in a report commissioned by Mandela's predecessor F.W. de Klerk.

The 1992 report was prepared by General Pierre Steyn, then the military chief of staff, and also implicated two other generals -- then defence force chief Kat Liebenberg, and Joffel van der Westhuizen.
In his statement Meiring denied he had seen the list and said all allegations implicating the three of them were false.
"On behalf of myself, General Liebenberg and Lieutenant General van der Westhuizen, I deny the allegations put forward during the TRC media conference yesterday," Meiring said.
No details of the Steyn report had been officially disclosed before this week and no substantive charges of human rights abuses have previously been publicly levelled against Meiring.
Mandela appointed him as an unsullied general with the loyalty of the white officer corps who would be able to lead his men into integration with their former guerrilla enemies.

Meanwhile state radio reported that parliament's defence committee would study the Steyn report and could call de Klerk to appear before it to answer questions about the alleged illegal activities of army generals.
Mandela set up the truth commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, with a mandate to investigate human rights abuses on all sides during the apartheid years.
